procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and Order dated 09.01.2020 of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in CRAD No.1063 of 2017.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh affirmed the conviction of accused Nos. 4, 5, and 6 (the appellants) for offenses punishable under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC). The High Court's judgment was rendered in Criminal Appeal Nos. 1063 of 2017, 997 & 1043 of 2017.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: Accused Nos. 4, 5, and 6 (appellants), who were convicted by the Sessions Court and whose conviction was affirmed by the High Court, approached the Supreme Court to challenge the High Court's judgment and order dated 09.01.2020.

directions: appellants are ordered to be released forthwith if not required in any other case

issue.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants for offences punishable under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the IPC, based on the statement of PW-9 as an eyewitness to the crime, was justified.

facts: The conviction of the appellants by the lower courts was primarily based on the testimony of a single eyewitness, PW-9, who was the cousin of the deceased.
PW-9 did not name the appellants in the First Information Report (FIR) or in his initial statement to the police.
PW-9 admitted that he did not know the accused persons before the incident and only came to know their names after they were arrested and reported in the newspaper.
There was an unexplained delay of several hours in recording PW-9's statement; the incident occurred at 6:30 p.m., but his statement was recorded at 11:30 p.m.

PW-9's testimony contained numerous inconsistencies and glaring contradictions, including identifying individuals in court whom he had not previously named and giving conflicting accounts of the motorcycles used in the crime.
law: The evidence of an eyewitness must be of a "very sterling quality and calibre" to be considered reliable.
An eyewitness's testimony should instill confidence in the court and be of a nature that can be accepted at face value.
The prosecution bears the burden of proving the guilt of the accused beyond a reasonable doubt.
application: The Court applied the standard of "sterling quality" to PW-9's testimony and found it to be severely lacking.
The testimony was deemed unreliable because it was "shrouded with inconsistencies" and "glaring" contradictions.
The fact that PW-9 failed to name the appellants in the FIR, coupled with his admission that he did not know them beforehand, created serious doubt about the accuracy of his identification.
The unexplained delay in recording his statement further weakened his credibility as a witness.
The Court found that these significant lacunae in the prosecution's case, centered on the unreliability of its star witness, were not properly considered by the Trial Court and the High Court.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the conviction, concluding that it was not justified. The testimony of the sole eyewitness, PW-9, was riddled with inconsistencies and contradictions, failing to meet the high standard required for an eyewitness account. As the prosecution failed to prove the appellants' guilt beyond a reasonable doubt, their conviction was deemed a miscarriage of justice, unsustainable, and was therefore set aside, leading to their acquittal.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the conviction of the appellants for offences punishable under Section 302 read with Section 149 of the IPC, based on the statement of PW-9 as an eyewitness to the crime, was justified.
appellant_arguments: The eyewitness (PW-9) did not previously know the accused and only learned their names after their arrest was published in the newspaper, which creates reasonable doubt about the appellants' identity.
Appellants A-5 and A-6 were not residents of the village where the incident occurred, a fact not mentioned in PW-9's initial statement.
There was an unexplained delay in recording PW-9’s statement, as it was recorded at 11:30 p.m. for an incident that took place at 6:30 p.m., despite PW-9 being present.
The alleged confessional statement of appellant A-4 is inadmissible under Section 25 of the Evidence Act.
The confessional statement does not indicate any common object shared by appellant A-4 with the other assailants.

cases.case_name: Dharam Pal v. State of U.P.
cases.principle: To elaborate that Section 149 IPC has two parts: the first deals with an offence committed by any member of an assembly 'in prosecution of the common object', and the second part deals with cases where members of the assembly 'knew that the same is likely to be committed in prosecution of the common object'.
That there is no uniform, inflexible, or invariable rule for arriving at an inference from the totality of facts and circumstances, which varies from case to case.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A member of an unlawful assembly is vicariously liable for an offence committed by another member if it was done in prosecution of the common object, or if the members knew it was likely to be committed. The common object is not governed by a uniform or inflexible rule, but is an inference to be deduced from the totality of facts and circumstances of each case, including the nature of the assembly, arms used, and their behavior.
obiter: 'Fact' means and includes— (a) That there are certain objects arranged in a certain order in a certain place, is a fact. (b) That a man heard or saw something, is a fact. (c) That a man said certain words, is a fact. (d) That a man holds a certain opinion, has a certain intention, acts in good faith or fraudulently, or uses a particular word in a particular sense, or is or was at a speciﬁ ed time conscious of a particular sensation, is a fact.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The court concluded that the prosecution failed to prove beyond a reasonable doubt that the appellants shared a common object with the other members of the unlawful assembly. The evidence did not establish any motive for the appellants, as they were not involved in the prior quarrel, nor was there any evidence connecting them to the deceased or the co-accused. Furthermore, no overt act was attributed to the appellants, and the eyewitness (PW-9) admitted that only one co-accused, Pawan, had caused the fatal injury, which contradicted the theory of a group attack with a shared intent to kill.
legal_tests_applied: To convict a person under Section 149 IPC, the prosecution must establish with evidence that: firstly, the accused shared a common object and were part of an unlawful assembly, and secondly, they were aware of the offences likely to be committed to achieve that common object.

The common object of an unlawful assembly can be gathered from the nature of the assembly, the arms used by them, and the behaviour of the assembly at or before the scene of the occurrence, as an inference to be deduced from the facts and circumstances of each case.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution failed to prove that the appellants shared a common object with other members of the alleged unlawful assembly.
No motive could be attributed to the appellants, as the evidence showed they were not involved in the prior fight that allegedly led to the incident.
There was no evidence to connect the appellants with the deceased or the co-accused.
No overt act was attributed to the appellants.

The eyewitness, PW-9, admitted in cross-examination that none of the accused except one person (Pawan) had caused injury to the deceased and that only a single shot was fired, which undermined the case for vicarious liability under Section 149.
policy_considerations: The non-consideration of the lacunae in the prosecution's case by the Trial Court and the High Court resulted in a miscarriage in the administration of justice, leading to a wrongful conviction that could not be sustained.
